impact.why: Read/write and execute as the desktop owner across local account separation.

likelihood.why: Requires a local foothold or another local account, not Internet exposure.

reachability.attacker: Different local OS account with loopback TCP access; no same-user privilege escalation asserted.
reachability.entrypoint: Loopback graph and terminal HTTP routes
reachability.summary: Requires another local OS account/process with loopback access while the engine is running and Python available. Arbitrary remote browser origins are rejected.

attackPath.summary: A local account connects to the engine, uses accepted loopback Host/Origin headers, selects or creates an idle bound graph, and opens and writes to its terminal.

codeEvidence.explanation: The only global request gate validates Host and Origin values; a native TCP client controls both and supplies an accepted pair.
codeEvidence.label: Browser guard accepts caller-selected headers

codeEvidence.explanation: A routed caller can launch a PTY process in the bound workspace under the engine's OS account.
codeEvidence.label: Privileged terminal creation

codeEvidence.explanation: Input supplied by the same unauthenticated caller is written directly to that shell.
codeEvidence.label: Terminal command input

confidence.rationale: Parent traced the shared route guard, graph API, terminal spawn and stdin sink; absence of any session credential is explicit.

originalCandidates.counterevidence: Loopback-only binding, Host and Origin validation protect ordinary remote websites. Random port is not client authentication. Opening terminal is intentional for owner.

originalCandidates.remediation: Per-launch IPC-delivered credential on all API reads/writes/SSE or private per-user authenticated native transport.
originalCandidates.title: Unauthenticated loopback terminal permits cross-account code execution

findings.remediation: Authenticate every private API read, write and stream with an unpredictable per-launch capability delivered through trusted native IPC, or use a private per-user transport with peer identity checks. Retain Origin/Host checks and remove developer origins from packaged mode. Do not place the capability in URLs or logs.
remediationTests: Missing, wrong, expired and previous-launch credentials fail on graph, terminal, provider, memory, execution and SSE routes.
A separate OS account cannot access the running owner's engine.
Packaged mode rejects localhost developer origins.

rootCause.summary: The shared `enforceBrowserBoundary` gate checks browser headers but establishes no client identity. `route` dispatches to graph and terminal handlers after this gate. Terminal workspace validation verifies directory existence and execution state, then spawns a shell and accepts stdin; it never authenticates the caller as the desktop owner.

severity.rationale: Owner-privileged command execution crosses local OS account separation; requires local host access rather than an Internet-reachable service.

findings.summary: A different local OS account with loopback access can forge the accepted Host and Origin headers, list or create a graph, and open and write to the desktop owner's terminal. The server authenticates no client.
findings.title: Unauthenticated loopback terminal permits cross-account code execution

counterEvidence: Loopback-only binding, Host and Origin validation protect ordinary remote websites. Random port is not client authentication. Opening terminal is intentional for owner.
limitations: No cross-account or live desktop exploit was executed; local TCP reachability is required. Same-user clients are not claimed as an OS privilege escalation.
validation.summary: Parent verified loopback-only binding, the explicit auth:none session route, accepted same-origin calculation, terminal workspace checks, process spawn and input sink. A different local account can construct the accepted headers without accessing an owner credential.

dataflow.summary: workspace cwd -> python3 -u -c -> default Python cwd module lookup -> import pty -> owner-privileged repository code before shell input.

impact.why: Arbitrary code execution under the desktop account.

likelihood.why: Depends on opening an attacker-provided project terminal.

reachability.attacker: Repository author supplies pty.py; owner binds repository and opens Terminal.
reachability.summary: The attacker controls ordinary repository content; the user must select that repository and open Terminal. No approved AI execution is required.

attackPath.summary: An attacker supplies a repository with pty.py; the user binds it and opens Terminal; the bridge imports that file as the desktop owner.

const PTY_BRIDGE = String.raw`
import os, pty, select, sys, signal, errno, struct, fcntl, termios
pid, master = pty.fork()
if pid == 0:
    shell = '/bin/zsh' if os.path.exists('/bin/zsh') else '/bin/sh'
    os.execv(shell, [shell, '-f', '-i', '-o', 'NO_BANG_HIST', '-o', 'NO_ZLE'] if shell.endswith('zsh') else [shell, '-i'])
codeEvidence.explanation: Importing pty can resolve repository-controlled pty.py before the intended shell is started.
codeEvidence.label: Bridge imports standard library

codeEvidence.label: Python launched in repository

confidence.rationale: Fixed import and spawn arguments establish current-directory module resolution; Python command-line documentation confirms the missing isolation behavior.

evidence.code:
const PTY_BRIDGE = String.raw`
import os, pty, select, sys, signal, errno, struct, fcntl, termios
pid, master = pty.fork()
if pid == 0:
    shell = '/bin/zsh' if os.path.exists('/bin/zsh') else '/bin/sh'
    os.execv(shell, [shell, '-f', '-i', '-o', 'NO_BANG_HIST', '-o', 'NO_ZLE'] if shell.endswith('zsh') else [shell, '-i'])
const child = spawnImpl('python3', ['-u', '-c', PTY_BRIDGE], { cwd: workspacePath, env: cleanEnvironment(environment), stdio: ['pipe', 'pipe', 'pipe'], detached: true });

originalCandidates.remediation: Trusted Python with isolated -I startup; inert shadow-module regression.
originalCandidates.title: Opening an untrusted workspace terminal imports attacker-controlled Python modules

findings.remediation: Run a trusted Python interpreter in isolated mode (`-I`) for the PTY bridge, or import only from a trusted startup directory before changing the child shell into the workspace. Keep repository content and user site packages out of bootstrap imports.
remediationTests: Opening Terminal in a fixture with inert pty.py and select.py does not import either file or produce a marker.
Normal shell startup, cwd, input, interrupt and shutdown behavior still pass.

rootCause.summary: `assertWorkspace` returns the bound repository path. Terminal creation uses it as Python cwd with `-u -c`; `PTY_BRIDGE` immediately imports `pty`. A clean environment removes PYTHONPATH but not Python's default current-directory search path, so repository source can shadow the expected standard library.

severity.rationale: An untrusted repository author can cause owner-privileged execution on terminal open, before the user submits a shell command.

findings.summary: Terminal startup invokes Python with `-c` in the selected repository. The bridge imports `pty` before starting the shell, allowing a repository `pty.py` to run immediately when the user opens Terminal.
findings.title: Opening an untrusted workspace terminal imports repository Python modules

counterEvidence: Fixed source/argv, stripped PYTHONPATH, zsh -f do not remove Python -c current directory lookup. Requires opening terminal in supplied repository.
limitations: No malicious module was executed; requires the user to open Terminal in an attacker-controlled repository.
validation.method: parent source trace and official Python command-line reference
validation.summary: Parent verified the bridge imports, spawn arguments and environment allowlist. Python -c prepends the current directory unless isolated/safe-path options apply.

dataflow.summary: Git indexed descendant -> lexical containment -> ancestor symlink resolution -> engine file read -> captured artifact -> accepted completeNode output

impact.why: External data can be misattributed to the project and enter stored/shared execution context.

likelihood.why: Requires a suitable filesystem layout and an accepted execution for onward persistence.

reachability.attacker: Untrusted repository content or generated workspace changes
reachability.summary: Requires attacker influence over workspace contents during an authorized execution and an engine-readable external target. Runtime reproduction proves the reader boundary; accepted receipt and later node consumption are additional prerequisites.

attackPath.summary: A workspace mutation replaces a tracked directory with a symlink to engine-readable data outside the workspace. The indexed descendant passes lexical containment and enters artifact capture; accepted outputs may persist and be included in later dependency context.

codeEvidence.explanation: resolve and relative reject textual traversal but do not resolve a symlink in an ancestor directory.
codeEvidence.label: Artifact path remains lexical

codeEvidence.explanation: lstat rejects a leaf symlink but follows an ancestor link. The resulting external regular file passes the checks and readFile reads its bytes.
codeEvidence.label: Final-component check follows ancestor symlinks

codeEvidence.explanation: Git's cached file path can survive replacement of its parent with a symlink; final-component lstat makes the external descendant appear regular in the manifest.
codeEvidence.label: Indexed descendant also enters manifest

codeEvidence.explanation: Once an execution satisfies receipt validation, captured file contents are passed to completeNode for durable persistence; dependency context can later include these artifacts.
codeEvidence.label: Accepted artifact reaches durable node output

confidence.rationale: Parent reproduced both manifest inclusion and artifact content capture with a temporary Git fixture and an inert external canary.

originalCandidates.counterevidence: Direct symlink leaves handled; deployed Codex sandbox policy may prevent creating certain links. Cross-workspace artifact containment failure is the claim; arbitrary sandbox privilege escalation is not.
originalCandidates.dataflow: Tracked capture/id_rsa remains in git index after capture becomes symlink to external directory; lexical resolve/lstat/readFile follows ancestor link, captures outside bytes, persists artifact and passes dependency context.
originalCandidates.title: Workspace artifact capture follows parent directory symlinks

previousFindings.remediation: Enforce canonical containment for every ancestor and the opened file in both manifest and artifact reads; use no-follow or descriptor-relative traversal with race-resistant checks. Reject paths whose parent chain escapes the pinned workspace, including tracked paths. Perform bounded reads on verified handles.
remediationTests: A tracked descendant under an ancestor symlink to an inert external file is rejected or skipped in both manifest and artifact capture.
Race changing an ancestor between validation and open cannot include external bytes.
Direct symlink behavior, ordinary contained files and receipts continue to work.

rootCause.summary: `git ls-files --cached --others` supplies indexed descendant names even after an ancestor directory changes to a symlink. Both manifest capture and artifact reading use lexical containment and final-component lstat. Ancestor symlinks therefore redirect the engine's file read outside the selected project. Accepted node outputs then persist the returned contents.

severity.rationale: A workspace-controlled ancestor link crosses the intended project artifact boundary and can copy engine-readable external data into artifacts. Persistence and onward provider context require an accepted execution.

previousFindings.summary: The workspace manifest and artifact reader validate lexical paths and only lstat the final component. An indexed path under a directory replaced with a symlink can read an external file and include its contents as a project artifact.
previousFindings.title: Workspace artifact capture follows symlinked directories outside the project

counterEvidence: Leaf symlinks are recorded as links in manifests and excluded as artifact files.
An accepted receipt is required before server persistence; creating the symlink alone does not automatically exfiltrate data.
limitations: No user files or secrets were accessed.
No live Codex run or provider exfiltration was performed.
Any claim of escaping the Codex OS sandbox depends on its effective filesystem policy and is not asserted.
validation.method: parent static trace plus inert local fixture reproduction
validation.summary: In a temporary Git repository, tracked capture/canary.txt was replaced by an ancestor symlink to a sibling fixture directory. The manifest still included capture/canary.txt, changed paths included it, and artifact reading returned the external canary with no skipped record. Fixture cleanup completed.
